extracted.intended_audience: students of algebraic geometry (Math 216); advanced undergraduates and graduate students reading Vakil's notes
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, numerical criteria, and geometric characterizations for line bundles, maps to projective space, and curve classification (genus 0,1,2,3, hyperelliptic, etc.) as presented in Vakil's chapter on curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality for curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohomology duality: for an invertible sheaf F on a curve C, hi(C, F) = h1−i(C, ωC ⊗ F∨) (relates h0 and h1 via the dualizing sheaf ωC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to translate statements about line bundles of nonpositive degree into statements about high-degree line bundles (and vice versa). Example: no sections of L∨ when deg(L∨) < 0 implies a formula for h0(L) via Riemann–Roch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative degree line bundles have no nonzero section
rubrics_metrics.description: If deg L < 0 then h0(C, L) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: any regular (no poles) section would force number of zeros ≥ 0, contradicting negative degree. See Important Exercise 18.4.C for divisor-counting viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree zero line bundles: h0 is 0 or 1 and triviality test
rubrics_metrics.description: If deg L = 0 then h0(C, L) ∈ {0,1}; moreover if h0(C, L) = 1 then L ≅ O_C (i.e., the line bundle is trivial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: a nonzero regular section has neither zeros nor poles, so div s = 0 and gives an explicit trivialization. Conversely for geometrically integral projective varieties h0(O) = 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-degree h0 formula (via Riemann–Roch/Serre duality)
rubrics_metrics.description: If deg L > 2g − 2 then h0(C, L) = deg L − g + 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows since L∨ ⊗ ωC has negative degree (ωC has degree 2g−2), so h1(C, L) = 0 and Riemann–Roch yields the formula. Important numerical rule to remember.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twisting by a degree-1 point changes h0 by at most one
rubrics_metrics.description: For a k-rational (degree 1) point p, h0(C, L) − h0(C, L(−p)) is either 0 or 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: use the short exact sequence 0 → L(−p) → L → L|p → 0 and the fact H0(C, L|p) has dimension 1; follow the long exact sequence in cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical criterion for base-point-freeness
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is algebraically closed and for every closed point p we have h0(C, L) − h0(C, L(−p)) = 1, then L is base-point-free (i.e., for every p there exists a section not vanishing at p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: for each p there is a section whose value at p is nonzero. Consequence: L gives a morphism C → projective space (Theorem 16.4.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of two points by a linear series
rubrics_metrics.description: For distinct degree-1 points p and q, the difference h0(C, L) − h0(C, L(−p − q)) ∈ {0,1,2}; if it equals 2 then the linear series separates p and q (i.e., the induced map f satisfies f(p) ≠ f(q)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently there exist independent sections vanishing at p but not at q (or vice versa); concretely h0(L) = h0(L(−p)) + 1 = h0(L(−q)) + 1 = h0(L(−p−q)) + 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of tangent vectors at a point
rubrics_metrics.description: If for a degree-1 point p one has h0(C, L) − h0(C, L(−2p)) = 2 then the map corresponding to L separates tangent vectors at p (i.e., the cotangent map is surjective / nonzero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: there is a section vanishing to order exactly 1 at p but not to order 2, which produces a function on the image vanishing to order 1 but not 2 on pullback, implying surjectivity onto the 1-dimensional cotangent space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for very ampleness (closed embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is algebraically closed and for all closed points p and q (not necessarily distinct) one has h0(C, L) − h0(C, L(−p − q)) = 2, then L gives a closed embedding of C into projective space (i.e., L is very ample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combines point-separation and tangent-separation criteria: separating all points and tangent vectors yields an embedding (Theorem 19.1.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree thresholds for base-point-freeness and very ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is algebraically closed and deg L ≥ 2g then L is base-point-free; if deg L ≥ 2g + 1 then L is very ample (gives a closed embedding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numerical consequences follow from the earlier twisting and high-degree h0 formula; memorize these degree bounds for line bundles on curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampleness criterion for line bundles on curves
rubrics_metrics.description: On a projective, regular, integral curve over k, an invertible sheaf L is ample if and only if deg L > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a blunt purely numerical criterion for ampleness on curves; generalizes to higher dimensions via Nakai–Moishezon but on curves it's simply positivity of degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of genus 0 curves with a rational point
rubrics_metrics.description: If C has genus 0 and admits a k-valued (degree 1) point, then C ≅ P1_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses L = O(p) of degree 1: h0(L) = 2 gives a closed embedding into P1_k, and the only closed embedding of a curve into P1_k is an isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 0 curves are conics (degree 2 embeddings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every genus 0 curve can be embedded in P2_k as a conic: L = ω∨_C has degree 2 and (for genus 0) gives a closed embedding into P2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus genus 0 curves over algebraically closed fields are isomorphic to plane conics (and to P1 if they have a k-point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-1 line bundles on non-P1 curves have at most one section
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is not isomorphic to P1_k and L is an invertible sheaf of degree 1, then h0(C, L) < 2 (i.e., at most one section).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there were two independent sections they would provide a degree-1 finite map to P1, forcing an isomorphism; used to distinguish P1 from other curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of degree-1 line bundle for points
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective regular geometrically integral curve C not isomorphic to P1_k and degree-1 points p and q, O_C(p) ≅ O_C(q) if and only if p = q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of the previous proposition: degree-1 line bundles identify points uniquely on non-P1 curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hyperelliptic curve (degree-2 cover)
rubrics_metrics.description: A (projective regular irreducible) genus g curve C is hyperelliptic if it admits a degree-2 (finite) morphism π: C → P1_k (the hyperelliptic map).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When g ≥ 2 this double cover (if it exists) is essentially unique (Proposition 19.5.7). Equivalently (Exercise 19.5.B) existence ↔ a degree-2 invertible sheaf L with h0(C, L) = 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperelliptic Riemann–Hurwitz count
rubrics_metrics.description: Over an algebraically closed field of char ≠ 2, a degree-2 cover π: C → P1 by a genus g regular curve has exactly 2g + 2 branch points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the special case of Riemann–Hurwitz for double covers; used to construct hyperelliptic curves branched over 2g+2 points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness of double covers branched at prescribed points (even r)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given r distinct points p1,...,pr on P1 with r even (over algebraically closed field of char ≠ 2), there is precisely one double cover branched exactly at those points (explicit model y^2 = f(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via y^2 = ∏(x − pi) on affine patches; special gluing considerations at infinity depending on parity of r; see Proposition 19.5.2 and explicit two-affine description (19.5.2.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-definition twist obstruction for double covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Over non-algebraically closed k (char ≠ 2), a double cover of A1 is of form y^2 = a f(x); different a differing by a square in k× give isomorphic covers, so double covers with same branch points can differ by classes in k×/(k×)^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: branch points alone may not determine the cover over non-closed base fields; this classifies twists of the cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between hyperelliptic line bundle and canonical sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: If L corresponds to a hyperelliptic cover C → P1, then L⊗(g−1) ≅ ωC (i.e., the (g−1)-fold tensor power of the degree-2 line bundle is the dualizing sheaf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses composing the hyperelliptic map with the (g−1)th Veronese embedding: the pullback gives at least g sections, and by Exercise 19.2.A the only degree 2g−2 sheaf with ≥ g sections is ωC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of hyperelliptic structure for g ≥ 2
rubrics_metrics.description: For genus at least 2, a curve admits at most one degree-2 cover of P1; equivalently, if L and M are two degree-2 line bundles giving maps to P1 then L ≅ M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recover the hyperelliptic map from the canonical map (ωC) and the rational normal curve image; this shows uniqueness of hyperelliptic map and associated L.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moduli/count of hyperelliptic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperelliptic curves of genus g ≥ 2 correspond to unordered 2g+2 distinct points on P1 modulo automorphisms of P1 (dimension heuristic: 2g+2 − dim AutP1 = 2g − 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a plausibility/dimension-count statement (needs rigorous moduli language to be precise) but useful as heuristic for 'space of hyperelliptic curves'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 2 curves are hyperelliptic and correspond to 6 branch points
rubrics_metrics.description: For genus g = 2, ωC has degree 2 and 2 sections and is base-point-free, giving a canonical double cover C → P1; hence every genus 2 curve is hyperelliptic and corresponds (in char ≠ 2) to a double cover branched at 6 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: there is a 3-dimensional family of genus 2 curves (heuristic) and every genus 2 curve arises from a degree-2 invertible sheaf with two sections (the dualizing sheaf here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical linear series for genus 3: embedding vs hyperelliptic
rubrics_metrics.description: For genus 3, ωC is base-point-free with 3 sections and gives a map to P2. If C is non-hyperelliptic this canonical map is a closed embedding (C is a plane quartic); if C is hyperelliptic the canonical map factors as a double cover onto a rational normal curve and is not an embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for embedding: check whether there exist p,q with h0(ωC) − h0(ωC(−p−q)) < 2 (equivalently existence of a degree-2 divisor with 2 sections indicates hyperellipticity). Converses: quartic plane curves give canonical models for non-hyperelliptic genus-3 curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 4 canonical model: lies on a quadric and is complete intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-hyperelliptic genus 4 curve has ωC of degree 6 with 4 sections, so the canonical image in P3 is a sextic curve that lies on at least one quadric; in fact such curves are complete intersections of a quadric and a cubic, and conversely such complete intersections give genus-4 canonical curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension counts via H0(P3, O(2)) and Sym^2 H0(C, ωC) show existence of quadrics vanishing on C. Analyze quadric type (cone, regular) to deduce properties; conversely, regular complete intersections of quadric and cubic are genus 4 non-hyperelliptic curves.
